numbers.headline: In a 12-week trial for a weed problem, people who cut down grew less anxious and less depressed, and slept better.
numbers.mirror: You fear life without weed will feel anxious and empty.
numbers.counted: adults in a treatment trial for a weed problem

basis.design: follow-up inside a 12-week medicine trial (secondary analysis)
basis.who: adults aged 18–50 diagnosed as dependent on weed (older DSM-IV criteria), in a 12-week medicine trial (NAC or dummy pill, both with cash rewards for clean urine tests)
basis.n: 302 adults (152 whose use went down, 150 whose use went up)
basis.measured: changes in anxiety, depression, sleep quality and quality of life, next to changes in weed use

numbers.caveat: This is cutting down, not only quitting. Overall quality of life did not improve in 12 weeks. The changes were small, and it is a link, not proof.
numbers.weak: A link found after the fact inside one trial; the mood changes were small.

ref.cite: Hser YI, Mooney LJ, Huang D, et al. (2017). Reductions in cannabis use are associated with improvements in anxiety, depression, and sleep quality, but not quality of life. Journal of Substance Abuse Treatment.
ref.quote: These results indicate a longitudinal relationship between reductions in cannabis use and improvements in anxiety, depression, and sleep quality.

numbers.origin: 07-mirror-stats/cannabis.json after '12 weeks' (figure, basis and ref kept; abstract refetched from Europe PMC on 2026-11-05)

problems: basis.when gives only 'published 2017'. The trial ran from January 2014 to April 2015.
basis.where says 'USA (UCLA-led)'. The data come from six US sites in the NIDA CTN ACCENT trial, and UCLA authors did only this secondary analysis.

basis.who says 'in a trial for cannabis use disorder'. The source is stricter: everyone had a DSM-IV diagnosis of cannabis dependence. All got NAC or placebo on top of cash rewards for clean urine tests and medication management. That context belongs in the basis.

Everything else holds. n=302 (152 reduction vs 150 increase, by the slope of weekly use days). The reduction group showed greater falls in anxiety and depression and better sleep, but not quality of life. The quote is word for word, 18 words. Headline: 21 words, 1 figure. Mirror: 10 words, second person. Note: 'the changes were small' is the drafter's reading of small coefficients; the paper does not say it.
check1.applied: Applied on 2026-11-05: the reviewer's corrections word for word.

gaps.note: Filled with 63% (people who beat a weed problem who no longer use it), which shows the route taken, not which route works. No study was found that compares relapse after stopping with relapse after cutting down among people who had been hooked on weed (the kind of figure the alcohol page's '27% vs 7%' gives).
gaps.searched: Europe PMC: cannabis/marijuana + remission/recurrence/persistence + abstinence/non-abstinent/moderation/controlled use; cannabis quit vs reduce. Seen: Lozano 2006 (Addiction, PMID 17034438, 291 treatment-seekers; people reached the goal they picked, abstract has no figures, full text paywalled), Stea 2015 (PMID 26168224, 119 recovered; abstinent recoveries had worse histories, no figures in abstract), Brezing 2018 (PMC5846101, 62 people, quality of life, no simple figure), Levin 2021 (PMC8282674, trial reduction categories, no stop-vs-cut figure), Farmer 2015 (PMC4229487, recurrence 27.7% but not split by continued use), Hughes 2016 (daily users, tag 'heavy', not allowed in the helps group; used under how-abrupt).
gaps.later: Our r/leaves harvest already counts relapse posts by day (103 of 221 after more than a month off; 'I can moderate now' named most). A count of moderation-try posts and how they ended could fill this later as a self-hooked number.

gaps.note: No medicine beat a dummy pill for being off weed (Cochrane 2025), so the '1 in N' form the kind asks for does not exist. Shown as '0 pills'.
gaps.searched: Cochrane 2025 (PMID 41025421) abstract refetched; no single trial was taken over the review.
